Article Title: In 2019, Chip and Joanna Gaines bought Waco’s neglected Cottonland Castle; after years restoring the 6,176-sq-ft landmark, the ‘Fixer Upper’ property listed for $2.7 million has found a buyer
Article Text:
The castle's transformation became a television project when the Gaineses documented the renovation for their 2022 Magnolia Network series Fixer Upper: The Castle.

A 135-year-old Waco landmark

From neglected property to TV project

The latest property move

A new chapter for the castle

For years, Cottonland Castle stood as one of Waco's most intriguing landmarks, an imposing historic home that had plenty of character but needed someone willing to take on the work. In 2019, that someone was Chip and Joanna Gaines. After years spent restoring and reimagining the property, the famous Waco couple's castle has now found a buyer, states an online report by PEOPLE. The Historic Waco Castle, also known as Cottonland Castle, went pending on Sept. 18 after being listed for $2.7 million in June. The eventual sale price has not been disclosed. The Gaineses had previously explored selling the property through an auction in 2023, adds the online report.As per PEOPLE, the castle dates back roughly 135 years and occupies 6,176 square feet. The four-bedroom, four-bathroom residence combines the imposing character of a historic structure with the highly considered interiors associated with the Gaineses' Magnolia brand. Its restoration focused on preserving the property's historic identity while making the house functional as a modern home. Antique tile floors, diamond-paned windows and other period details remain central to the design, adds the report.Inside, the layout includes a formal dining room and a spacious great room, along with more distinctive spaces such as a card room, library and conservatory. Together, the rooms give the house a character that is unusual even among historic Texas properties, the online report elaborates.The castle's transformation became a television project when the Gaineses documented the renovation for their 2022 Magnolia Network series Fixer Upper: The Castle.The show followed the couple as they tackled the challenges of bringing the aging structure back to life. For Chip Gaines, the property had long been a personal ambition. He had reportedly followed the castle for years, making repeated attempts to acquire it whenever it returned to the market. The restoration ultimately became one of the couple's most ambitious projects, combining architectural preservation with the layered design approach that has become synonymous with Fixer Upper.The castle is not the only Waco property the Gaineses have been dealing with this year. Around the same time Cottonland Castle was listed, the couple also put their Colonial-style Hillcrest Estate on the market for $1.7 million. The five-bedroom, four-bathroom property had previously been offered as a short-term rental through Airbnb and the Magnolia website. It remains listed for sale, according to property records.The Gaineses have also taken on another notable restoration project involving an abandoned factory building that was transformed into the Gristmill. The property, which viewers may recognize from Joanna Gaines' Magnolia Table cooking show, was listed for $935,000 and remains on the market.The pending sale marks the latest chapter in Cottonland Castle's long history. What began as a neglected historic property became a high-profile restoration project and a television centerpiece before returning to the real estate market.With a buyer now lined up, the 135-year-old landmark is set to move into its next era, carrying with it the architectural details and history that made the Waco castle worth saving in the first place.Images Courtesy: EOnline and People
Article Summary: The Historic Waco Castle, also known as Cottonland Castle, went pending on Sept. 18 after being listed for $2.7 million in June. The castle's transformation became a television project when the Gaineses documented the renovation for their 2022 Magnolia Network series Fixer Upper: The Castle.

Article Title: Cornell University gang-rape case: DA reveals new disturbing details as investigation reopens
Article Text:
Cornell University in Ithaca, New York

Also Read |

Cornell supports reopening investigation

(With AP inputs)

The district attorney (DA) who has reopened his investigation into an alleged 2024 sexual assault at Cornell University has defended his earlier decision not to prosecute anyone, citing the former student’s own account of the incident to police.In several media interviews on Tuesday (local time), Tompkins County DA Matthew Van Houten argued that while the male students involved did things that were “morally wrong”, the woman’s initial account of the incident to police did not include allegations that she was drugged, incapacitated beyond the ability to consent, or forced to engage in sexual activity.“She went to the police because she knew it wasn’t right,” Van Houten told CNN.“There were no question marks. There was no additional need to find information because we had all of the information that the police collected from Jane Doe through her very detailed, very comprehensive statement that she provided,” he added.Van Houten has not released the complainant’s sworn statement to police, but instead made public a summary that includes some of her direct quotes. He also defended his office’s decision not to conduct further investigation after the woman, identified in court filings by the pseudonym "Jane Doe," initially spoke to police.The woman filed a lawsuit this month alleging that she was assaulted by seven male students at the Chi Phi fraternity house on Cornell’s campus in October 2024. According to the lawsuit, the alleged incident occurred after she was pressured into taking drugs and consuming alcohol, leaving her unable to consent to sexual activity.The complainant reported the incident to Cornell’s campus police, but Van Houten’s office decided not to prosecute anyone at the time. The office later reopened the criminal investigation amid growing public attention over the woman’s allegations.Cornell University has expressed support for reopening the criminal investigation, saying in a statement that its own inquiry had resulted in disciplinary action against some students, including expulsions.According to the statement, the Chi Phi chapter remains barred from campus.The woman’s lawsuit accuses the university of failing to prevent the alleged assaults and of not adequately addressing sexual violence on campus. It includes a photograph that purportedly shows a group chat between fraternity members discussing the events of that night.Van Houten dismissed the photograph as a “red herring”, arguing that it had no bearing on the legal assessment of whether the woman had consented or whether there was evidence that she had been unable to consent under state law.“We received it, but it was not relevant to the assessment of whether Jane Doe consented or whether there was any evidence of lack of consent on her part as defined by the penal law,” he said.
Article Summary: DA Matthew Van Houten has reopened his investigation into an alleged 2024 sexual assault at Cornell University. He has defended his earlier decision not to prosecute anyone, citing the former student's own account of the incident to police. The woman filed a lawsuit this month alleging that she was assaulted by seven male students at the Chi Phi fraternity house on Cornell’s campus in October 2024.

Article Title: A farmer left $10.9 million to build a cancer centre; Mayo Clinic was supposed to get it only if the local hospital lost its independence
Article Text:
A farmer's $10.9 million will with two conditions

Radiation proved impossible

Mayo's challenge

Iowa Supreme Court affirms on standing

Iowa farmer Herman Carl Stille died in September 2020 at 94, leaving an estate worth about $10.9 million. His 2017 will directed the remainder to Floyd County Medical Center (FCMC) in Charles City to establish a cancer centre for local residents. It also named the Mayo Foundation as the alternative recipient, for Alzheimer's research, if the hospital lost its independence and became part of a major healthcare corporation. Mayo went to court after the hospital found it could not provide radiation treatment. On May 1, 2026, the Iowa Supreme Court ruled in favour of the medical centre.Stille was a cattle farmer and factory worker before he retired. He never married, had no children and left no living siblings or other identified heirs. He received care at FCMC for more than a decade and was the largest donor to the hospital's charitable foundation.He was also a Mayo patient in Rochester, Minnesota, and had given to its charitable foundation. His last gift there came in January 2017. He stopped donating because he was dissatisfied with the care he received, and his later gifts went to FCMC alone.The $10.9 million estate was mostly farmland. After several small charitable bequests, his will, signed in August 2017, gave the remainder to the hospital for a cancer centre.It required an oncologist on staff, office and consultation space, a family area and separate areas for radiation, chemotherapy and other treatments. The gift was contingent on the hospital staying independent. If it lost its independent status and joined a major healthcare corporation, the remainder would go to Mayo Foundation for Alzheimer's research.Attorney Michael Kennedy, who drafted the will, testified that Stille added the independence requirement in 2017. Stille's earlier will, from 2011, had no such condition and named Mayo as the backup only if the cancer centre could not be established. Stille's sister had died from Alzheimer's complications, and he feared facing the same disease.After Stille's death, FCMC began planning the centre, expecting roughly $10 million from the estate. Administrators soon realised they could not provide on-site radiation. Radiation requires a linear accelerator, which is costly and heavily regulated. In Iowa, a hospital needs a certificate of need, and one is generally not issued when radiation facilities already operate within a certain radius. Several hospitals near FCMC already offered radiation. The machine is also expensive to run, and FCMC lacked the patient base to afford its upkeep.The hospital said the centre could still satisfy the other requirements. It proposed to staff an oncologist through cooperation or subcontracting with other facilities, and to transport patients to another facility for radiation. It also noted that more cancer patients are treated with chemotherapy than with radiation.Mayo asked the court to rule that the gift to FCMC had failed. It argued that the will's conditions went beyond independence, and that the money should pass to it if FCMC could not build the centre Stille described. Kennedy testified that Stille's intent was for the money to go to Mayo if either condition was unmet.FCMC countered that it had remained independent, so the trigger for Mayo's gift had never occurred.The Chickasaw County district court, after a three-day bench trial, ruled for FCMC in June 2025. It found that the hospital was independent and that its planned centre would meet five of the six specifications, all but radiation. The judge concluded that Stille cared more about the hospital's independence than about how the centre would operate, and would not have withdrawn the bequest had he known radiation was impossible.Mayo appealed, and the Supreme Court retained the case. On May 1, 2026, it unanimously affirmed, in an opinion by Justice Thomas Waterman. Justice Mansfield took no part.The court did not adopt the district court's reasoning. It found no ambiguity in the will, which conditioned the gift to Mayo on FCMC's loss of independence. Because FCMC remained independent, and Mayo did not dispute that, the court held that Mayo takes nothing under the will. A beneficiary whose condition has not occurred lacks standing to challenge the gift to someone else, so the court affirmed on that basis alone and did not reach the remaining issues.The court noted that FCMC still has a legal and moral obligation to use the funds as intended. Mayo cannot enforce it, but the Iowa attorney general has standing to enforce the terms of charitable trusts.The ruling ends a dispute that began in 2021 and leaves the remainder of the $10.9 million estate with FCMC. The hospital says it will proceed with the Stille Cancer Centre on its campus. It says it is still unclear which cancer services will be available, including how radiation care will be provided for patients who need it.
Article Summary: Iowa farmer Herman Carl Stille died in September 2020 at 94, leaving an estate worth about $10.9 million. His 2017 will directed the remainder to Floyd County Medical Center (FCMC) in Charles City to establish a cancer centre for local residents. It also named the Mayo Foundation as the alternative recipient, for Alzheimer's research, if the hospital lost its independence and became part of a major healthcare corporation. Mayo went to court after the hospital found it could not provide radiation treatment. On May 1, 2026, the Iowa Supreme Court ruled in favour of the medical centre.

Article Title: In 2006, 18-year-old mariachi singer Elisa Gastellum died before moving to Las Vegas; 20 years later, 27 scholarships in her name have helped 10 recipients become mariachi teachers
Article Text:
​For Elisa's parents, Terri and Bob Gastellum, remembering their daughter eventually became about more than preserving memories. They wanted to create an opportunity for other young musicians to pursue the path Elisa had envisioned for herself.

Turning grief into a legacy

A brother continues the journey

Twenty years of impact

A song that keeps moving forward

Some dreams end before they have the chance to begin. For Elisa Gastellum, mariachi music was more than a pastime. The Arizona teenager had found a place for herself on stage, where performing allowed her personality and love for the music to come through. In 2006, at just 18, Elisa was preparing to move to Las Vegas with her older brother, Javier. The siblings imagined building lives around mariachi, with Javier hoping to teach and Elisa looking toward singing and furthering her education. The plans never came to pass and a car crash in Arizona claimed Elisa's life before she could make the move. She died instantly, leaving her family with the grief of losing a daughter and sister whose musical ambitions were only beginning to take shape, states an online report by Fox5Vegas.For Elisa's parents, Terri and Bob Gastellum, remembering their daughter eventually became about more than preserving memories. They wanted to create an opportunity for other young musicians to pursue the path Elisa had envisioned for herself. And that's when they established the Elisa Gastellum Memorial Foundation, a scholarship program dedicated to supporting young mariachi musicians in Las Vegas. What began as a way to honor an 18-year-old singer has since become a source of practical help for students trying to keep music in their lives while pursuing their education.The foundation's support extends beyond scholarships. Young musicians can also receive assistance with instruments and lessons, as well as opportunities to attend mariachi conferences that allow them to develop their skills and connect with the wider mariachi community, states the report.According to the report, Javier eventually made the move to Las Vegas that he and Elisa had once planned. He became a mariachi teacher at Gibson Middle School, where he has spent two decades working with young musicians. His career has given Elisa's legacy a living connection to the next generation. Every student who learns to sing, perform or play mariachi under his guidance represents another continuation of the musical world the siblings once imagined entering together.For Javier, teaching has become closely tied to keeping that family connection alive. His work is not simply about music lessons; it is also about helping young people discover their abilities and giving them a reason to believe that music can have a lasting place in their lives.The foundation's reach has grown steadily since Elisa's death. It has now awarded 27 scholarships in her name to young mariachi musicians in Las Vegas. Remarkably, 10 of those recipients have gone on to become mariachi teachers themselves, claims the online report. That number gives the scholarship program a significance beyond financial assistance. The students who received help are now helping build the next generation of musicians, creating a cycle in which one young singer's unfinished dream continues through others.Among those recipients is Ervin Garcia, a Las Vegas mariachi musician who received financial support for his education. For Garcia, the scholarship helped make college more accessible at a time when paying tuition would have placed a significant burden on his family. He never met Elisa, and she never knew his name. Yet nearly two decades after her death, her name has become part of his musical journey.Elisa's life lasted only 18 years, but the musical legacy created in her name has continued for two decades. From scholarships and instruments to classrooms and mariachi conferences, the foundation has helped turn remembrance into opportunity. The most striking part of that legacy may be the teachers. Ten scholarship recipients have returned to the mariachi community as educators, passing the music forward to students who may one day do the same. A dream that stopped in 2006 has, in a different form, continued to grow—one musician, one classroom and one scholarship at a time.Images Courtesy: istock and Facebook
Article Summary: Elisa Gastellum died in a car crash when she was just 18 years old. Her parents wanted to create an opportunity for other young musicians to pursue the path Elisa had envisioned for herself. Elisa's Memorial Foundation has awarded 27 scholarships in her name to young mariachi musicians in Las Vegas.

Article Title: 2,100-year-old shipwreck filled with 122 varieties of ancient Roman tableware found by archaeologists in Turkey was mentioned in a letter by Roman statesman Cicero
Article Text:
A shocking shipwreck

Significance of Rhosus tableware

Off the Turkish coast near Adrasan, marine archaeologists recently discovered the remains of an ancient cargo ship bound for Rome and loaded with thousands of pieces of tableware in 122 different varieties, most famous and in demand at the time. The vessel had been carrying ceramic plates, bowls and serving dishes when it sank some 2,100 years ago, as per a report by All Things Interesting.Researchers believe the cargo originated from the region around the ancient port city of Rhosus, in modern-day Arsuz, Turkey, which served as a hub for elite tableware production at the time. Rhosus tableware was so well known and in demand that the Roman statesman Marcus Tullius Cicero famously mentioned ordering it in a letter from 50 B.C.E.According to an announcement about the discovery made by Turkey's Minister of Culture and Tourism, Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, excavations on the shipwreck began in 2025. Since then, marine archaeologists have recovered thousands of ceramic pieces, which have been transferred either to the Antalya Museum or to conservation labs.The wreck, sitting at depths between 140 and 18 feet, revealed 122 distinct types of tableware of different forms and sizes.Due to the wreck's deep location, the team had to use underwater robotic systems to support the marine archaeologists' work on the ocean floor.The ship dates back 2,100 years and was transporting thousands of ceramics, packed together for shipment across the Mediterranean. The 122 distinct dish types also provide a detailed window into the variety of tableware available in the ancient world.Moreover, it reveals how ceramics were packed and distributed at the time. For instance, the ceramic pieces found in the shipwreck were packed with clay between them before being placed inside crates, in order to reduce the risk of them breaking while at sea.For the researchers, this packing method also aided in preserving the tableware for years after the ship sank, allowing modern experts to get insights from it that they might not otherwise be able to.During the Late Hellenistic and Early Roman period, much of the Mediterranean's fine tableware was produced in the port of Rhosus in present-day Turkey. Historians are aware of this due to the various written records left behind by the Romans.Rhosus was mentioned, for instance, in a letter from the famous orator Cicero to his close friend Titus Pomponius Atticus, which he wrote while he was governor of Cilicia in about 50 B.C.E. In the note, Cicero wrote that he had ordered Rhosica vasa, which means vessels or dishes from Rhosus.In the centuries following the discovery of that short reference to these ceramics, archaeologists and scholars have debated the exact production site of Cicero’s tableware. Some scholars have suggested that Cicero’s ceramics may have been what’s known as Eastern Sigillata A, popular ancient clay tableware originating somewhere along the Gulf of İskenderun in southeastern Turkey, but the debate has continued.Although it remains unknown who ordered the newly found tableware shipment, the recent shipwreck discovery provides important physical evidence of the region's thriving maritime economy in ancient times. A similar shipwreck was also found filled with hundreds of well-preserved ceramics. Other marine archaeologists diving elsewhere in Turkey’s waters have also discovered a 1,500-year-old wreck carrying 10,000 ceramic plates, as well as a 1,100-year-old ship that sank with jugs of olive oil aboard.
Article Summary: Marine archaeologists recently discovered the remains of an ancient cargo ship bound for Rome and loaded with thousands of pieces of tableware. The vessel had been carrying ceramic plates, bowls and serving dishes when it sank some 2,100 years ago. Researchers believe the cargo originated from the region around the ancient port city of Rhosus, in modern-day Arsuz, Turkey, which served as a hub for elite tableware production.

Article Title: World’s “grumpiest cat” moved into a Ladakh couple’s home with 3 kittens; family gave up their house so she could raise them
Article Text:
Image: Puskar Basu/ Discover Wildlife

A wild cat moves into a Ladakh couple’s home with 3 kittens

Why the cat chose the house

The "grumpy" face hides a highly adapted predator

She left the house every morning to hunt

The kittens leave before the camera can find them

Built for extreme cold

A habitat under pressure

Hanle has become an important place for sightings

A remarkably elusive Pallas's cat has chosen an unexpected nursery in the high-altitude village of Hanle in Ladakh. The female entered a local couple's home through an open window and settled there with three kittens. Farmer Tsering Topgyal and his wife, Palmo, alerted the Forest Department after discovering the wild cat and her young. Rather than disturbing them, the couple reportedly left their house and stayed with relatives elsewhere in the village while the mother raised her kittens. Wildlife photographer Puskar Basu later spent four weeks observing the female from a hide outside the barricaded property. He documented an unusual encounter between one of the Himalayas' most secretive small cats and a human settlement.The encounter happened in Hanle, a remote village at about 4,500 metres above sea level. The settlement lies amid a stark Trans-Himalayan landscape of rocky slopes, marshes and snow-fed streams. Despite its harsh appearance, the area supports wolves, foxes, marmots, pikas, raptors and the elusive Pallas's cat.According to Basu's account in Discover Wildlife, Tsering and Palmo came face to face with an unusual cat that had entered their home through an open window.Tsering then glimpsed three kittens.The couple contacted the Forest Department, which advised them not to disturb the animals. They gave up the house and stayed with relatives on the other side of the village. A caption in Basu's article says the house was vacated for two months. The Forest Department also placed a barricade around the property to keep people away.The arrangement gave the female a quiet place to raise her young while still letting her leave the building to hunt.The location mattered. The house stood on the edge of Hanle, away from much of the activity in the settlement. Nearby marshland offered voles and pikas, which are important prey for Pallas's cats.The species normally uses natural shelters and abandoned burrows rather than buildings. The IUCN Cat Specialist Group says Pallas's cats depend heavily on rock cavities and burrows dug by other animals, including marmots. The Hanle house offered a mother with kittens a protected den close to a productive hunting ground.It was not the first time a Pallas's cat had used a building near Hanle. A naturalist's trip report from July 2022 described a female using an abandoned building as a den site. The observers were later told that she had kittens inside.Pallas's cat, Otocolobus manul, is known for its broad face, low-set rounded ears, short legs and dense coat. Those features earned it the nickname "the world's grumpiest cat". The name describes its appearance, not its temperament.Its body is adapted to the extreme cold of Central and South Asia. It has a compact, stocky build, and Basu describes its fur as the longest and densest of any cat, which helps it survive the brutal winters.The species ranges from parts of Central Asia through Mongolia and China and into the Himalayan region. In India, confirmed records include Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim and, since a 2025 survey reported the first photographic evidence, Arunachal Pradesh.A 2026 study in Oryx documented the first confirmed occurrence of the species in Karakoram Wildlife Sanctuary in northern Ladakh. It relied on DNA analysis of a scat sample collected at 4,424 metres. The researchers also identified pika and Himalayan marmot remains in the sample, which gives some evidence of the cat's diet in the region.Basu spent weeks watching the female from outside the barricade. She would leap out of the window early in the morning and spend four to five hours hunting in the surrounding marsh. She returned to her kittens in the afternoon.He saw two main hunting strategies. She would creep towards prey she had spotted, or sit and wait outside a burrow for an animal to emerge. Basu also saw her rattle her tail as a distraction once prey had been startled, which bought her time to pounce.He estimated that she needed five or six rodents a day, and that reaching that quota took 20 to 30 attempts. These observations relate to the one female he followed and are not a measure of the species as a whole. Research from the Himalayan region names pikas, voles and Himalayan marmots as likely key prey.The marshes around Hanle also produced an unusual observation. Pallas's cats generally live in dry, rocky, open country and have little apparent need to swim. But the marshes here are unusually deep, and Basu watched the female enter the water. He suggested this might be the first documented swimming behaviour in the species.Basu had hoped to photograph the three kittens once they were old enough to venture out. That moment never came. One morning he arrived and found the female gone. He believed she had left the previous night, probably helping the kittens out through the window they had used as their den.The disappearance meant the family could finally return home. Basu searched around Hanle for the kittens but could not find that family again.During his wider search he did find another Pallas's cat kitten hiding in a rocky den. He watched it from about 30 to 40 metres for two days as it played, explored the rocks and interacted with its mother.The Pallas's cat looks bigger than it is. It typically weighs 2.5 to 4.5 kg, but its dense fur exaggerates its size. Basu reports that in winter it adds a layer of fat and dense fur, which can double its weight. Temperatures in parts of its range can fall to around -40°C.Its short legs let it keep a low, crouched profile while hunting. Combined with its muted coat, this makes the cat very hard to spot against rocky terrain.The species is generally found between roughly 3,000 and 5,000 metres. The IUCN Red List assessment notes a scat record at 5,593 metres in the Nepal Himalaya, the highest recorded so far.The Pallas's cat has a wide range, but its populations are often sparse and fragmented. The latest global IUCN Red List assessment classifies it as Least Concern, based on the 2019 assessment published in 2020. The IUCN's first Green Status assessment of the species, published in July 2026, rates it "Indeterminate", which reflects substantial uncertainty about its population.Habitat degradation and fragmentation, loss of prey, infrastructure development, livestock grazing and disturbance are among the main concerns. The cat's reliance on burrows and rock shelters also makes it dependent on suitable refuges.Free-ranging dogs are another concern. Basu writes that they hunt Pallas's cats in packs and are increasing rapidly around Hanle. He also notes that construction in the marshland has reduced that habitat by about half over two decades. He says construction there has now stopped.The Pallas's cat is rare enough in the Indian Himalayas that individual observations can add meaningful information about its distribution. Researchers have recorded the species around Hanle, Staklung and Lal Pahari in the Changthang region.Sightings have also become more frequent in parts of Ladakh as wildlife tourism has grown. Conservationists quoted by Mongabay say that more visitors, and so more eyes on the landscape, is one likely reason. They also point to prey availability and possibly higher breeding success, though they say the link is uncertain and needs more research.Tsering and Palmo could have reclaimed their home the moment they found the animals. Instead they followed the Forest Department's advice, stayed elsewhere and let the mother raise her kittens undisturbed. When the cats moved out, Palmo returned home and got back the view from the window that had served as the cat's entrance and exit.
Article Summary: Wildlife photographer Puskar Basu spent weeks observing the Pallas's cat. The female entered a local couple's home through an open window. She left the house every morning to hunt. The house stood on the edge of Hanle, away from much of the activity.

Article Title: An Indiana man planned one Hobbit house; seven years later, he had built an 11-building fantasy village from recycled and secondhand materials
Article Text:
PC: Free Press Indiana News

How did one Hobbit house become an 11-building fantasy village

PC: Free Press Indiana News​

How did one Hobbit house become a popular Indiana attraction

What can visitors expect at Indiana’s Hobbit Festival

How will this Indiana Hobbit village become a medieval town

Rick Sparks never intended to build a village. The Tolkien fan originally planned a single Hobbit-inspired house on a 3½-acre property outside Connersville, Indiana, as a weekend getaway. Seven years later, that house has become his residence, and the site has grown into Rackshire, an 11-building fantasy village. Its Tolkienesque rounded doors, turf-covered roofs and stone fireplaces are built largely from recycled lumber and secondhand materials. Sparks bought the property in 2018 for about $17,000. His first festival in 2021 drew more than 3,000 people over three days, and he now envisions 15 to 20 more buildings.According to the Free Press Indiana News, Sparks' interest in Tolkien's "The Hobbit" and "The Lord of the Rings" goes back to childhood, when he first learned about the fictional, peaceful creatures and the cosy, round underground homes they inhabited. He remembers watching the Rankin/Bass animated adaptations of Tolkien stories in the late 1970s and early 1980s, then reading Tolkien's books and playing Dungeons & Dragons.His children grew up with it, too. His daughter, Kyla Robinson, recalls her father collecting "Lord of the Rings" memorabilia and making props he could not buy, adding that she has always called him a fabricator.The idea of a Hobbit-style home arose years later, when Robinson, after marrying and considering buying a house, asked her father whether it would be fun to live in one. Sparks started drawing plans. Robinson ultimately decided to buy a conventional house rather than wait for him to build one, but Sparks carried on with the project. The article says he uses his years of experience as a builder and former owner of a landscaping company to do most of the work himself. Sparks, 53, works as a live-in caregiver for people with disabilities, a schedule that gives him every other week off and plenty of uninterrupted time for construction.The first house was supposed to be the end of the project, but curiosity seekers began stopping by to see it. Sparks added two smaller structures in 2020, featuring Hobbit elements favoured by his son and daughter, and then kept experimenting and building from scratch until he had a village. He eventually built a semicircular driveway, partly because so many strangers were stopping that they needed an easier way to get back onto the highway. "I get people to stop pretty much daily," Sparks said.One of those visitors was Monica Osting, a "Lord of the Rings" fan from Greenville, Ohio, who spotted a photograph of the house on a Facebook group devoted to Middle-earth. The article says she learned it was only about a 90-minute drive from her home, contacted Sparks and visited. She later volunteered to create Rackshire's website, giving Sparks a way to promote the village without relying almost entirely on Facebook and word of mouth. According to the report, Sparks organised his first festival in 2021, and more than 3,000 people attended over three days, including visitors from surrounding states and as far away as Pennsylvania. Some waited as long as 90 minutes to get inside the main house. Robinson said last year's festival drew more than 2,000 people, and organisers used a handheld clicker to count admissions and had improved arrangements for parking and moving people onto the property.FPI News listed the Hobbit Festival, a celebration of Tolkien Week, as scheduled to run from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Sept. 26 and 27 at 4428 W. State Road 44, Connersville. Tolkien Week always falls near Sept. 22, known as Hobbit Day, the shared fictional birthday of the characters Bilbo and Frodo Baggins. Admission was listed at $5 per person, cash only, with parking also $5, cash only, at a neighbouring farm at 4684 W. State Road 44. The site's hilly terrain may not be suitable for those with mobility issues. Sparks had been recruiting vendors whose goods fit the setting, including pottery, leatherwork and armour, medieval-style clothing, woodworking, honey and blacksmithing. Robinson planned to sell fall concessions including homemade cider, caramel apples and pumpkin rolls, and costumes were encouraged but not required.According to the report, Sparks envisions adding as many as 15 to 20 more small buildings to create something resembling a permanent medieval village, with shops for vendors, a central courtyard and a 24-foot bell tower. He is developing overnight accommodations and hopes the property can attract groups interested in Dungeons & Dragons and other fantasy gaming. He has also begun developing a gaming store, is taking reservations for overnight stays in the main house, and has discussed a nine-hole fantasy-themed miniature golf course with small waterways and bridges. Sparks said his main goal is to provide for others the kind of escape Tolkien's tales gave him as a boy.
Article Summary: Rick Sparks originally planned a single Hobbit-inspired house on a 3½-acre property outside Connersville, Indiana. Seven years later, that house has become his residence, and the site has grown into Rackshire, an 11-building fantasy village. Sparks bought the property in 2018 for about $17,000. His first festival in 2021 drew more than 3,000 people over three days.

Article Title: Russia backs India's claim to UNSC seat, firmly shuts door on Germany & Japan
Article Text:
Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly (Photo: Reuters).

Russia on Saturday backed a permanent seat for India and Brazil on the United Nations Security Council, while strongly opposing the same for Western countries.During his speech at the General Assembly, Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said no additional seats at the UNSC should be given to Western countries, especially to Germany and the US ally, Japan.Russia has been one of the most consistent supporters of India’s bid for a permanent seat on the UN Security Council . Moscow has repeatedly backed India’s candidature as part of a broader push to make the Council more representative of Asia, Africa and Latin America.Lavrov has previously argued that the current composition no longer reflects today’s global balance and explicitly endorsed India, alongside Brazil, for permanent membership.This support was reiterated in the 2026 BRICS New Delhi Declaration, with China and Russia backing India and Brazil for a greater role in the UN, including the Security Council.Lavrov accused the West of continuously pumping weapons into Ukraine while helping target drones and missiles at Russia's civilians and civilian infrastructure.He also mentioned that Europe raised an anti-Moscow regime in Kyivv, in order to control the Russian influence."To pursue a utopian goal of containing Russia, the West dismantled the European security system and cultivated a Russophobic regime in Kyiv," he said, while warning the Western nations of "consequences".He further accused Europe of doing everything to block a peaceful settlement with Ukraine and disrupt negotiation prospects favoured by many, including the Trump administration.Lavrov claimed several EU leaders of being infected with racial superiority, encouraging the rise of what he called Ukrainian Nazism.The Russian foreign minister said the UN’s core principles were being put at risk, with the West overlooking the spread of Nazism in Ukraine.
Article Summary: Russia has been one of the most consistent supporters of India's bid for a permanent seat on the UN Security Council. Moscow has repeatedly backed India’s candidature as part of a broader push to make the Council more representative of Asia, Africa and Latin America.

Article Title: Student protests rock France with over 400 detained: Why are schools protesting - explained
Article Text:
File photo: A student walks past a burning bicycle next to the Baggio High School, blocked in protest of the government's release of next year's draft budget, in Lille, France

Students take protests beyond Paris

Civil servants join nationwide strike

Why the budget is at the centre of the anger

Poll Vote & Share your view Which area should receive greater priority in France’s upcoming budget? Education Healthcare Public Safety Infrastructure 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

France was hit by a nationwide wave of strikes and student protests, with civil servants walking off the job and high school students blocking hundreds of schools as anger over budget cuts, overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages spread across the country.The mobilisation came two days before Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu's government is due to present its draft 2027 budget, which includes a planned €54 billion savings drive. The protests have added to pressure on the government as it tries to rein in France's finances ahead of next year's presidential election.The unrest was particularly visible at schools, where students piled up bins and barriers to prevent access. The education ministry said around 400 schools were affected by protests or disruptions on Tuesday, out of roughly 3,700 nationwide. More than 440 people, most of them minors, were detained, according to interior minister Laurent Nuñez.​​At least 10 teachers, several students and 48 law enforcement officers were also injured during Tuesday's unrest, according to officials.The school protests began in the Paris region last week but have since spread to cities including Lille, Lyon, Nantes, Marseille, Bordeaux and Rennes.Students have been protesting over a shortage of teachers, overcrowded classrooms, poor school conditions and demanding timetables. At some schools, however, the demonstrations escalated into clashes with police.In Lille, rubbish bins were set on fire outside the Lycée César Baggio, while police used tear gas and batons after protesters threw objects. Similar confrontations were reported elsewhere, although many blockades remained peaceful.At the Lycée Arago in Paris, students blocked the entrance with bins while a placard reading "Macron explosion" was displayed. Outside the Hélène-Boucher school, protesters put up a banner saying "Fewer cops, More money"."We want fewer police because we think there is a huge amount of police repression, both against high school student movements and social movements more generally," final-year student Mael Breton told Reuters.Students have cited teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and poor school conditions as key grievances. “There are 34 of us in each class, and it’s just not feasible. The teachers are overworked,” a 16-year-old student told AFP, saying the education system was “completely broken.”The government's response has been mixed. Lecornu condemned violence around schools but acknowledged that students' concerns over the education system needed to be heard and addressed. Education minister Édouard Geffray said students had a right to protest but condemned violence as "indefensible".The student mobilisation coincided with a broader strike by public-sector workers, including teachers, healthcare workers and firefighters.Unions organised more than 170 rallies across France to oppose the government's budget plans and its proposed freeze on state employees' base salaries in 2027. The CGT union has argued that repeated pay freezes have eroded workers' purchasing power.Firefighters were among those taking part after a summer of major wildfires exposed concerns over resources. The education ministry said just over 11% of teachers and other school staff were on strike, while participation among other civil servants was below 10%.Transport disruption was limited in the morning, although the aviation regulator warned of possible disruption at some airports.CGT leader Sophie Binet said the government had 48 hours to reverse the planned spending cuts before the union considers further strike action."This summer, who was on the front line? It wasn't the billionaires, the big bosses or the shareholders. It was civil servants and working people. And how are they being thanked? By cutting their pay? The anger is enormous," she told BFMTV.Lecornu's government is trying to find savings as France grapples with a mounting debt burden. The proposed €54 billion savings package is aimed at bringing the public deficit down, while the government has also warned that public debt could reach 121.7% of GDP in 2027.France's public debt reached €3.595 trillion at the end of June, or around 119% of GDP, according to national statistics agency Insee.The cost of servicing that debt is also rising. France is expected to spend around €79 billion on interest payments this year, with the government projecting the figure could rise to €91 billion in 2027.The government is therefore trying to cut spending while unions resist pay restraint and students demand more teachers and resources for schools.
Article Summary: Around 400 schools were affected by protests or disruptions on Tuesday. More than 440 people, most of them minors, were detained, interior minister says. At least 10 teachers, several students and 48 law enforcement officers were also injured. Unions organised more than 170 rallies across France.

Article Title: ‘Wake up’: Iran releases 25-page letter urging US voters to reject Trump ahead of midterms
Article Text:
The letter was released about five weeks before the US midterm elections

‘Wake up’: Iran takes message to US voters

‘Death to America’ explained as attack on rulers

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has made a direct appeal to American voters, urging them to reject President Donald Trump ’s policies and “wrest control back from corrupt politicians” as the US heads towards its midterm elections. In a lengthy open letter addressed to the American public, the powerful Iranian military force argued that Washington’s war against Iran had failed to achieve its objectives and called for a change in US policy towards Tehran.The 25-page letter, released seven months after the US-Israel war against Iran began, seeks to draw a distinction between the American people and their government. The IRGC argues that ordinary Iranians and Americans share common interests and grievances, portraying both as victims of political leaders pursuing costly wars. It also urges Americans to oppose US support for Israel and foreign military interventions, while presenting peaceful coexistence between Washington and Tehran as possible if US policy changes.IRGC spokesman Gen Hossein Mohebbi reinforced the message at a news conference in Tehran on Tuesday, saying the only way for the conflict to end was for Washington to acknowledge defeat and withdraw. He urged Americans to reconsider their leadership and put pressure on the Trump administration, arguing that many US citizens remained unaware of what he described as the “harms” caused by its policies.The timing of the letter is significant. The letter was released about five weeks before the US midterm elections, with the IRGC describing the current period as a moment when the American political system is at its weakest. Mohebbi said he did not necessarily expect the letter to change the US administration’s behaviour, but hoped American voters would hear its message.The letter repeatedly attacks Trump’s justification for the war, particularly his claim that Iran’s nuclear programme posed a threat that required military action. Tehran has consistently denied seeking nuclear weapons and maintains that its uranium enrichment programme has civilian purposes.“The enemy [US] knows that Iran is not after nuclear weapons,” Mohebbi said, echoing the letter’s argument that Washington has used the nuclear issue as a pretext to pursue wider strategic and economic goals.The IRGC also claims that the US and Israel failed to achieve their stated objectives in the war. According to the letter, the targets shifted repeatedly after earlier goals, including regime change and partition of Iran, were not achieved. It lists objectives ranging from forcing Iran’s unconditional surrender and destroying its nuclear and missile programmes to taking control of the Strait of Hormuz.The letter declares Iran the victor, claiming that thousands of US and Israeli strikes damaged Iranian infrastructure but failed to accomplish their stated aims. It further claims that Iranian forces inflicted major losses on US military assets and severely damaged American bases across the region. These assertions are presented by the IRGC as evidence of a broader strategic defeat for Washington.The Strait of Hormuz features prominently in the letter and Mohebbi’s remarks. He rejected US claims that Iran had lost its leverage over the vital waterway, arguing that the movement of a limited number of vessels did not mean the strait was fully open. Oil exports through the waterway, however, have recovered substantially from the levels seen earlier in the conflict, according to figures cited in the supplied material.The IRGC letter also attempts to explain one of the most recognisable slogans associated with Iran’s political system: “Death to America”. It argues that the phrase is directed at the US political establishment rather than the American population.“‘Death to America’ is a prayer for the eradication of the diabolical ruling elite whose seat of power is the White House,” the letter says.The document repeatedly contrasts the American public with Washington’s political leadership, claiming that taxpayers ultimately bear the financial burden of US wars. It asks Americans to question why their government continues to pursue military confrontation and warns of what it describes as the consequences of an ongoing conflict.The IRGC’s approach echoes Cold War-era efforts to reach an adversary’s population directly. During the Vietnam War, Vietnamese broadcaster Trinh Thi Ngo, widely known as “Hanoi Hannah”, used English-language broadcasts to target American troops, urging them to question their government and the war. Her programmes highlighted US casualties, anti-war protests and reports critical of the conflict while presenting the Vietnamese side’s narrative.Iran has similarly sought to communicate directly with Western audiences since the latest war began, using Iran-linked media and online networks, including English-language AI-generated videos, memes and short-form content.The IRGC letter now represents a much more formal version of that strategy: an attempt to speak past Washington and directly to American voters.For Tehran, the central message is that the war is not simply a military confrontation between two states, but a political choice that Americans themselves can challenge. Mohebbi urged them to put pressure on their government, while the letter concluded with a broader argument that Iran’s resistance had demonstrated the limits of American military power.Meanwhile, Iran’s economic pressures remain severe. The rial fell to a new record low on Tuesday, with traders in Tehran reportedly exchanging more than 2.5 million rials for one US dollar. The currency has repeatedly hit new lows since the war began.
Article Summary: Iranian military force argues that Washington’s war against Iran had failed to achieve its objectives. Letter urges Americans to oppose US support for Israel and foreign military interventions, while presenting peaceful coexistence between Washington and Tehran as possible if US policy changes. Letter released about five weeks before the US midterm elections.

Article Title: In 2024, 75-year-old Iowa farmer Evie Haupt said three wind turbines on her 160 acres were bringing in about $35,000 a year while using under 3 acres and had helped reduce $350,000 in farm debt to $67
Article Text:
A financial lifeline for rural landowners

The explosive expansion of Iowa wind power

Addressing local pushback and debate

On a 160-acre farm in central Iowa, three tall wind turbines quietly rise above the fields. Each turbine uses less than an acre of land, but together they provide an annual income that has changed the financial future of 75-year-old farmer Evie Haupt. According to a CBS News report by Janet Shamlian and Alicia Hastey, Haupt earns about $35,000 each year by leasing part of her land for the wind turbines. The income rises with inflation and has helped her pay down a $350,000 farm debt left after her husband died a decade ago. Her remaining debt is now $67,000. For many family farms across the United States, extra sources of income have become important lifelines. The U.S. Department of Agriculture expects farm profits to fall by 25 per cent, as farmers face higher costs, changing crop prices and unpredictable weather. Adding wind power to traditional farming can provide steady income and help protect farmers from financial shocks.Farm debt can leave families with difficult choices, including selling land that has been in the family for generations. Haupt faced this situation after her husband died and left her with hundreds of thousands of dollars in farm debt.Payments from the wind turbines provided her with a regular source of income that she could use to repay the loans. Each turbine takes up less than an acre, allowing Haupt to continue farming most of her 160 acres. This means the same land provides her with two sources of income while only a small portion is used for the turbines. The payments can also increase over time because the contracts include inflation adjustments, helping landowners manage rising prices and other costs. For Haupt, the arrangement has made a significant difference. She has now paid off more than 80% of her farm debt while continuing to use the land for farming.Iowa has become a major wind energy state over the past two decades. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, Iowa had only a few hundred wind turbines 20 years ago. Today, it has more than 6,000, producing about 60 per cent of the state's energy. Across the United States, more than 70,000 land-based wind turbines are operating, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. Nationwide, wind power supplies about 10 per cent of the electric grid. Federal energy officials also say current U.S. wind power cuts carbon emissions by an amount equal to taking 73 million passenger vehicles off the road. Attorney Kathy Law, who grew up on a farm and married a farmer, has helped place nearly half of Iowa's wind turbines. Her work in energy law grew from her own family's experience with farming. Law wanted to study law while she was in high school, but the severe farm crisis of the 1980s kept her home to help with the family farm. She later went to law school in her forties. She graduated on the same day her son finished high school and later served as president of the Iowa Wind Energy Association for three years. "From my farm background, I think I can talk their talk and have conversations with landowners that are interested in having wind turbines on their property," Law told CBS News.The rapid growth of wind power in rural communities has also brought opposition in some counties. Local critics say wind turbines can change scenic views, create unwanted noise and threaten birds and bats. Law believes landowners should be able to decide what happens on their property. "Nobody's requiring them to put that on their farms or on their land," Law said during her interview with CBS News. "We want to be able to put turbines on our land and receive those benefits. " Haupt has a similar view of the changes to her farm. While she remains attached to traditional farming, she sees clean energy as an important step for rural communities. "I look at it as progress," Haupt told CBS News. "I think we can't stand in the way of progress." For Haupt, giving up a very small part of her land to produce electricity makes sense for her finances and for the wider community. "I need to give up one or two acres of my land so that I can generate a commodity that we all use every day, and we all want to use more of it every day," Haupt said. "So I'm happy to be able to be a part of that generation."
Article Summary: Iowa has become a major wind energy state over the past two decades. More than 70,000 land-based wind turbines are operating in the U.S. Nationwide, wind power supplies about 10 per cent of the electric grid. Critics say wind turbines change scenic views, create unwanted noise and threaten birds and bats.

Article Title: In 2018, Malibu residents stayed after a mandatory evacuation during the Woolsey Fire; their volunteer group was credited with saving dozens of homes
Article Text:
The large smoke plume from the fire encroached on Malibu as seen from the Pacific Coast Highway. Credits - Wikipedia

Why neighbours stayed in

Inside the volunteer push

The burn scar of the fire in and above Malibu in aerial view alongside map showing the spread of the Woolsey fire across Malibu. Credits - Wikipedia

The brigade model that came after

Leave as soon as an evacuation order is issued. One of the most well-known instances was the 2018 Woolsey Fire in Malibu, California, which influenced how one of the country’s largest fire agencies views residents who stay behind. The fire began on Nov. 8, 2018, near the Santa Susana Field Laboratory above Simi Valley, close to the Los Angeles-Ventura County line, and reached Malibu early the next day. The Los Angeles County After Action Review documented the combination of factors, the rapid spread over the 101 motorway, and a warning to the public that agencies will not always be immediately available. At the time, a volunteer group of homeowners known as the Point Dume Bomberos remained behind after the required evacuation and battled spot fires, and neighbours credited them with helping protect homes in the area.The Woolsey Fire burnt 96,949 acres and destroyed 1,643 structures, according to California state records. Three people were killed. A mandatory evacuation order was issued for all of Malibu on Nov. 9, yet as the fire tore through the hills, some residents questioned whether enough fire resources were available.The county review helps explain why the official response was stretched. The review said the Woolsey Fire struck while the Camp Fire was raging in Northern California, and other emergencies were drawing from the same limited pool of firefighting resources.That contributed to delays in getting large numbers of engines into Malibu. The study also pointed out deficiencies in communicating evacuations to the public.Some residents said their knowledge of the local streets and terrain helped them understand where fires were developing and where they needed help. For others on Point Dume, a headland most people never thought to burn, that vista proved costly.Even with volunteers on the ground, the fire drew close. About 90 homes were lost on the Point, roughly 15% of its 610 properties, The Malibu Times reported.The group took its name from an older Point Dume surf team known as the Bombers. A phone call among surfing friends brought together about 15 people within hours, and as the days passed, the number climbed to some 2. They used hand tools, a water truck and dirt motorcycles and walkie-talkies to stay in touch when phone coverage failed. One of the organizers prepared a map and, using binoculars from a lookout point, spotted flare-ups and radioed the others with their approximate locations.One member, Sam McGee, told CNN the crew put out at least 100 hot spots in five days and got nine hours of sleep out of 144. McGee also cautioned against taking all the credit, saying that luck helped some residences. He said there were no further structure fires after the first bad night. Local accounts credited the group with helping protect homes from spot fires and flare-ups.Fire science can help explain why such patrols may be important. A USDA Forest Service report by US Forest Service scientist Jack Cohen discovered that the large flames of strong wildfires don’t immediately ignite homes beyond 100 feet. The ignitions are from things close to the house, mainly smouldering embers and small surface fires that are igniting items close to the house. A house can survive a fire that passes at full strength if there is someone to smother the little ember fire on a deck or in a gutter.Their support was more than just firefighting. The same group also helped bring in food and water when the road was closed and supplies were running low, and later they ran a relief facility in a school car park near Point Dume. Members of the Bombers also decided that the experience should not depend on luck next time.A 2026 report from the Natural Hazards Center at the University of Colorado Boulder, Trial by Fire , examined the Community Brigade pilot during the first seven days of the December 2024 Franklin Fire and January 2025 Palisades Fire in Malibu. Based on participant observations and interviews with brigade members and officials, the researchers reported preliminary evidence of greater trust, fire-risk awareness and community ownership.The report also distinguished between the two models. Community brigade volunteers undergo extensive training under the direction of the county fire department and the US Forest Service and are called into service when needed. That is unlike stay-at-home defenders who reject evacuation orders. Trained and coordinated volunteers bring local expertise to a professional response, whereas untrained residents who refuse to leave put themselves and the personnel that may have to rescue them in danger.For Malibu, the experience points to the value of preparation before a fire starts. Residents are still urged to evacuate when ordered, while organized community brigades can help share information, support evacuation and reduce ember-related risks under official direction. Homes with fewer combustible materials around them are better positioned to withstand wildfire, while communities that train and coordinate before an emergency are better prepared to respond safely.
Article Summary: The Woolsey Fire burnt 96,949 acres and destroyed 1,643 structures, according to California state records. At the time, a volunteer group of homeowners known as the Point Dume Bomberos remained behind after the required evacuation and battled spot fires. Local accounts credited the group with helping protect homes from spot fires and flare-ups.

Article Title: In 2017, a California wildlife-park owner defied a wildfire evacuation to protect 1,000 animals; by morning, he had lost no animal, bird or structure
Article Text:
Green Memorial Wildlife Park, California. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Evacuation order at Safari West, night of October 8, 2017

The preserve's animals: about 1,000 across 98 species, 2017

Lang's report: no animals or structures lost, home a mile away destroyed

NIST case study, 2007 Witch Fire: 74 of 245 homes destroyed in The Trails

California Agriculture survey, 2025: 505 producers, 65 percent sheltered in place or defended property

Black Fly Ride at West Midlands Safari Park. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

On the night of Sunday, October 8, 2017, a wildfire closed in on Safari West, a wildlife preserve near Santa Rosa in Sonoma County, and its 77-year-old owner, Peter Lang, remained there after officials ordered an evacuation. KQED reported that Lang said officials wanted everyone to evacuate and that he could not leave. Lang worked late into the night fighting small fires amid 1,000 animals or more. He stated that by dawn, he hadn't lost a single animal, bird, or building at the preserve, even though his own house had burned down a mile down the road. That account comes from Lang himself and has not been independently audited.According to The Washington Times, the preserve had emergency plans for earthquakes, floods and wildfires, including fires that could arrive with as little as three hours' notice, but officers arrived on Sunday night and gave the workers only 15 minutes to evacuate. The Visit California profile describes how Lang evacuated his wife, guests and employees, then stayed behind to defend the preserve. Alone on the grounds, he connected hoses to put out spot fires that started when embers fell into the grass. KQED reported that he also had to drive cornered nyala antelope through a ring of fire.The Washington Times reported that the preserve housed about 1,000 animals of 98 species, and Visit California listed giraffes, cheetahs, rhinoceroses and hyenas among them.Later sources give slightly different figures, but these numbers describe the preserve in October 2017. Lang bought the former ranch in the 1980s and turned it into a wildlife preserve. According to Visit California, he and his zoologist wife, Nancy, started a captive breeding program, and the preserve opened to visitors in 1993. The Washington Times also reported that about 150 employees worked at the preserve and at least 11 of them lost their homes in the fires.Lang, according to KQED, said that he had not lost any animal, any bird and any building, but he lost his house. On the day when the evacuation took place, Lang was at home with his wife one mile away from the reserve. The aviary was the most vulnerable of all buildings. Lang told KQED that if a burning branch had fallen on the aviary, it would have burned down. Some of the employees were able to get inside despite the fact that there was a power outage. Fred Dickerson, one of the employees, told KQED that they were able to account for every animal, even those that they released for flying. Fox News reported that Safari West posted on Facebook that its fences were still intact and that all animals were contained, accounted for and safe. KQED also reported that after the fire, Lang and his wife called the park their home.The National Institute of Standards and Technology examined a community affected by two 2007 fires in its report, A Case Study of a Community Affected by the Witch and Guejito Fires . The community, The Trails in Rancho Bernardo north of San Diego, had 274 homes, 245 of them within the fire perimeter. Of those, 74 were completely destroyed and 16 were partly damaged, according to NIST. The report describes ember attack, both direct and indirect, as a contributing factor in the destruction of homes in the community, and NIST's summary said embers ignited about two-thirds of the destroyed homes. The report notes that defensive measures had been taken at about one-third of the houses and that 15 of the 16 partly damaged houses had been successfully defended.The study Farming and ranching through wildfire: Producers' critical role in fire risk management and emergency response, published in California Agriculture in 2025, surveyed 505 California farmers and ranchers affected by wildfires between 2017 and 2023. Sixty-five percent of producers said they sheltered in place or defended their property at least once when a wildfire approached. Of those who evacuated, 75 percent returned as soon as possible to assess and reduce damage.Among the 146 livestock producers surveyed, 32 percent said they had to evacuate their livestock. The authors noted that evacuation can protect animals but can also add to their stress and health problems. In addition, 77 percent of the 303 producers near wildfires gave direct support to neighbors and emergency responders, and 47 percent said that support included creating firebreaks and defending properties directly.
Article Summary: Safari West, a wildlife preserve near Santa Rosa in Sonoma County, was evacuated on October 8, 2017. The preserve's owner, Peter Lang, 77, stayed behind to fight small fires amid 1,000 animals or more. Lang told KQED that by dawn, he hadn't lost a single animal, bird, or building at the preserve, even though his own house had burned down a mile down the road.

Article Title: In 2019, a Florida activist grew or foraged his food to test whether he could live without grocery stores; he completed one year without a grocery store
Article Text:
AI Representation: A garden with raised beds and freshly harvested vegetables, illustrating a food-growing setup in Florida. Image credits: Chatgpt

Food Freedom

: A Year of Growing and Foraging 100 Percent of My Food

Food Freedom project, November 11, 2018 to November 11, 2019

Project rules: no packaged, processed or shipped food

Protein and starch challenges, according to forager Hank Shaw, 2019

Honey harvest: 75 pounds from three colonies after 100 days

Vienna foraging survey: 458 residents, 64 percent of green space visitors

Ocean View Growing Grounds study, 2020: arsenic in chard, lead in strawberries

Grocery store. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

From November 11, 2018 to November 11, 2019, activist Rob Greenfield set out to see whether he could meet all of his food needs by growing or foraging for everything he ate. WUSF described how, for 365 days in Orlando, Florida, he avoided grocery stores, restaurants, takeout and food prepared by friends. He completed the project in November 2019 and later documented it in the book, as noted in National Geographic’s profile of Rob Greenfield.National Geographic reported that Greenfield learned which plants worked well in Florida by talking with local growers, visiting community gardens, attending classes, watching YouTubers and reading books about local and native flora. He explained that this preparation, done before the project began, took him from knowing little about growing food in the region to being able to grow and forage all of his food. Greenfield relocated from San Diego to Orlando for the project, where the nonprofit Orlando Permaculture provided support, according to a January 2022 WUSF profile. With no land of his own in Florida, Greenfield built a 100-square-foot tiny house from repurposed materials in the backyard of Orlando herbalist Lisa Ray, who offered him the space.Nothing packaged, processed or shipped became part of his food intake, according to the book's summary.Even vitamins and supplements were excluded. According to Greenfield's page on the project, he grew over 100 foods in his garden and over 200 foods in nature, including medicinal herbs and vitamins. The only thing he consumed but did not swallow was toothpaste, as he explained in an interview with WUSF.This has been termed the “forager’s dilemma” by Shaw, who is a forager and author of cookbooks in California. Protein had to be obtained from legumes in the absence of hunting and fishing, but the state of Florida has very few wild legumes. Greenfield fished a few times per month, kept his catch frozen, and included pigeon peas and southern peas. Yucca, yams, and sweet potatoes were his sources of starch.By the time of National Geographic's visit, more than 100 days into the project, Greenfield kept three honey bee colonies and had harvested 75 pounds of honey. He would also boil the salt from seawater. WUSF listed papaya, beets, spinach, sweet potatoes and moringa among the crops he raised. The rules governed the food he ate, and he also got an Instant Pot and containers to preserve the produce. The project page of Greenfield states that there were 15 gardens created for others, more than 200 fruit trees planted for the community, and more than 5,000 seed packs distributed free of cost. Some of this work began before the year started, so the figures cannot be taken as results of the 365 days alone.The study Urban nature at the fingertips: Investigating wild food foraging to enable nature interactions of urban dwellers, by Christoph Schunko and Anjoulie Brandner in the journal Ambio , surveyed 458 residents of Vienna, Austria. Among the surveyed residents who visit public urban green spaces, 64 percent had previously foraged for wild food. Foraging frequency was related to the targeted plant species and their life forms. People who foraged more often reported a stronger connection to nature, had more childhood foraging experience and lived on the outskirts of the city. Social acceptance and lack of access to wild foods were perceived as barriers. That figure covers green space visitors in one city, not all urban residents or all cities. The scale differs sharply from Greenfield's project, in which he foraged more than 200 foods over a year.The study Monitoring and mitigation of toxic heavy metals and arsenic accumulation in food crops: A case study of an urban community garden, published in Plant Direct in January 2020, repeatedly tested fruits and vegetables over four years at the Ocean View Growing Grounds community garden, on a formerly contaminated brownfield site in southeastern San Diego. Swiss chard grown directly in the ground contained arsenic at 0.80 mg/kg dry weight, while lettuce contained 0.42 mg/kg. Strawberries contained lead at 0.84 mg/kg dry weight. Tomatoes and Brussels sprouts showed no detectable levels of heavy metals or metalloids. Over the four-year sampling period, lead in the leaves of Black Mission fig trees measured 0.843 to 1.531 mg/kg dry weight, and in Mexican lime leaves 1.103 to 1.522 mg/kg dry weight, the study authors reported. When the raised beds made of uncontaminated soil were introduced, there were no detectable levels of heavy metals and metalloids in the crops.A Plantae summary of the same study, written by Mary Williams, noted that contaminants were found in the tree leaves but not in the fruits. The San Diego results do not describe the yards Greenfield used. Naturalist Steve Brill said in his interview with National Geographic that the lead settles in places where it is released, so he is careful about picking anything within 50 feet of heavy traffic. Greenfield told National Geographic that he never picks anything sprayed or contaminated. Phil Ackerman-Leist, an expert on pesticides, suggested that foragers in the city should use the same caution when gathering produce as they do while shopping at the produce aisle of a supermarket.
Article Summary: For 365 days, activist Rob Greenfield grew and foraged all of his food in Orlando, Florida. Greenfield documented his experience in a book called "Food Freedom" He avoided grocery stores, restaurants, takeout and food prepared by friends. He grew over 100 foods in his garden and over 200 foods in nature.

Article Title: In 2011, Gary Sinise launched his foundation to support military families; by November 2025, it had dedicated its 100th mortgage-free adapted smart home, giving wounded veteran Joe Bowser a new start
Article Text:
Gary Sinise Foundation dedicated its 100th mortgage-free, specially adapted smart home to Army veteran Joe Bowser (Image Credit: Gary Sinise Foundation )

The injury that changed Joe Bowser’s life

Why he kept saying no to a new home

The design includes five-foot-wide hallways, lower cabinets that can be reached from a wheelchair and an accessible shower fitted with a heated bench (Image Credit: YouTube/ Gary Sinise Foundation )

A home built around the way he lives

A milestone for the Gary Sinise Foundation

A friendship that became part of the story

For nearly two decades, wounded Army veteran Joe Bowser had turned down an offer that could have made everyday life much easier for him. That changed in November 2025, when the Gary Sinise Foundation dedicated its 100th mortgage-free, specially adapted smart home to him. According to the Gary Sinise Foundation’s own 2025 year-end campaign page, the milestone home was built around Bowser’s mobility needs, giving him and his wife, Michele, a safer and more accessible place to live. The milestone marked a major moment in the foundation’s work to provide specially adapted homes for severely wounded veterans.Bowser’s story goes back to his military service in Iraq. He had served in the Army and later returned to the reserves following the September 11 attacks . In 2004, he was deployed to Iraq, where a rocket attack in April that year left him with serious injuries to his right leg. Doctors initially tried to save the leg, but after several operations, amputation eventually became necessary. Adjusting to life after such a severe injury was not easy, but Bowser found a way to reconnect with something he enjoyed: ice hockey.He later took part in hockey programmes for veterans with service-related injuries. For Bowser, the sport offered more than a chance to play. It helped him regain a sense of normality and reconnect with an activity he enjoyed before his injury.It was in 2006 that he met Sinise, beginning a friendship that would continue for years.The offer of a specially adapted home did not immediately appeal to Bowser. In fact, he spent years turning it down. The Gary Sinise Foundation had considered Bowser for its R.I.S.E. programme, which provides custom-built homes for wounded veterans. In an interview with PEOPLE, Sinise said Bowser repeatedly suggested that another veteran should receive the opportunity instead. Sinise told PEOPLE that Bowser was among those veterans who did not necessarily believe their injuries were severe enough to warrant a specially built home. Eventually, however, Bowser agreed.The decision came as the limitations of his existing home became harder to ignore. His previous house in West Virginia was built in 1839 and had narrow hallways and doorways that were difficult to navigate in a wheelchair. The second floor had also become increasingly challenging and unsafe for Bowser. He sometimes uses a wheelchair when he cannot use his prosthetic leg, making the layout of the old house particularly difficult.The new Tennessee house was designed with those everyday challenges in mind. According to PEOPLE, the approximately 2,991-square-foot, three-bedroom, single-storey ranch near Fort Campbell was built so that Bowser could move throughout the home without having to deal with stairs. The design includes five-foot-wide hallways, lower cabinets that can be reached from a wheelchair and an accessible shower fitted with a heated bench. These may seem like small details, but for someone navigating a home with a prosthetic leg or wheelchair, they can change how easily everyday activities are managed.The idea behind the foundation's specially adapted homes is not simply to provide a veteran with a house. The homes are designed around the individual needs of the person who will live there, with accessibility and independence built into the design. For Bowser, that means being able to move around his home more easily and safely.Bowser’s house also marked an important moment for the Gary Sinise Foundation. The organisation dedicated its 100th mortgage-free adapted smart home to him in November 2025. Its campaign page describes the homes as specially designed for severely wounded veterans, with accessibility features intended to help recipients regain independence in their daily lives.The house also gives Bowser and Michele more room to spend time with their family. The couple have 10 grandchildren, and the new home provides a setting where family gatherings can happen without the accessibility barriers they faced in their previous house. For the foundation, reaching 100 homes represents more than a numerical milestone. Each project involves creating a home around the specific needs of a veteran whose life has been affected by a serious service-related injury.Bowser’s connection with Sinise has also become deeply personal over the years. According to PEOPLE, the two men became even closer after each experienced the loss of a son to cancer. Bowser’s son Justin died in November 2023, while Sinise’s son Mac died in January 2024. Sinise launched the Gary Sinise Foundation in 2011 to support service members, veterans, first responders and their families. His interest in supporting veterans was also influenced by his experience playing Lieutenant Dan in Forrest Gump and his desire to help veterans after their service.For Bowser, the new home provides a single-storey layout and accessibility features designed around his mobility needs, while giving him, Michele and their family more room to spend time together.
Article Summary: Gary Sinise Foundation dedicated its 100th mortgage-free, specially adapted smart home to Army veteran Joe Bowser. The home was built around Bowser’s mobility needs, giving him and his wife, Michele, a safer and more accessible place to live. The milestone marked a major moment in the foundation's work to provide specially adapted homes for severely wounded veterans.

Article Title: In 2000, a Colorado man gave up money to leave debt and financial motives behind; 12 years later, he was still surviving through foraging, gifts and discarded goods
Article Text:
